processing: Certified organic China-type leaf, handled in the usual Darjeeling way for black tea: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, lighter in spring.
harvest_season: First and second flush lots are both sold; the timing follows the usual Darjeeling calendar of spring and early summer, with an autumn picking.
appearance_dry: Typical of China-leaf Darjeeling: small wiry leaf, greener in spring and browner in summer.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in first flush and amber in second flush.
appearance_wet: Small mixed green and copper leaf, browner in later flushes.
taste_profile: A seller's account credits the garden's China bushes with a rose-like flavour. Otherwise expect the usual Darjeeling shift from floral spring teas to rounder summer ones.

brewing.notes: Western style. Cooler and shorter for first flush; a bit hotter for second flush.

vintage_note: Sold by flush and harvest year, often with a grade such as FTGFOP1 and an organic label; first flush lots such as 2026 appear on the market. Drink spring lots within about a year.
description:
Lingia lies in the Golden Top valley, about 30 kilometres west of Darjeeling town, and is planted with China-type bushes. Of its 220 hectares, 141 are under tea, on slopes reported from about 2,800 to 6,000 feet.

It is certified organic and belongs to the Chamong Group, a major organic producer in Darjeeling and Assam. The leaf is made in the normal regional way.

A seller's account claims a rose flavour no other garden can match. Take that as marketing, though a floral note is what to look for. Brew first flush gently and do not rush to add sugar.

Lots usually state flush, year and grade, and European sellers carry them under the garden name. Try a first and a second flush together to see the range.
history:
German missionary brothers J.A. and F.J. Wernicke are credited with establishing Lingia in 1867. Neighbouring Mariabong was once part of it, added to the Kyel estate as a wedding gift for Mary, a daughter of Lingia's owners, and its name means Mary's place in Lepcha.

The Chamong Group acquired Lingia from Williamson Magor in 2001.
